messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Elena, a 61-year-old bus driver for a municipal transit authority, still sees the man’s face when she closes her eyes. The accident happened two years ago, just after she’d pulled her bus away from a downtown stop. A car ran a red light and struck a pedestrian crossing the street. Elena watched the whole thing from her elevated seat—the man’s body folding, the blood pooling on the asphalt, the driver who did not stop. She remembers screaming into her radio for help, but no one came quickly enough. The man died before the paramedics arrived. She has not forgiven herself. She was certain that if she had jumped out of her bus sooner, if she had run into the street and somehow stopped the car, the outcome would have been different. She will never forgive herself for not doing more, and the thought that she should have protected a stranger—a failure she replays daily—has hollowed out the life she used to know.

In the months afterward, Elena began to notice that certain things would pull her back into that moment without warning. The sight of blood, even a small cut on her own hand, makes her stomach clench and her vision narrow. When she drives her route and sees a car hit another car, or merely hear the screech of brakes, her whole body goes rigid—she tastes metal, hears the man’s final breath, smells the hot asphalt. These episodes are not simply memories; they are complete relivings where the event feels present, not past. Sometimes the emotional storm arrives without any image at all—she will be standing in her kitchen and suddenly feel the full weight of helplessness and horror, even though no picture comes to mind.

To manage this, Elena has developed a set of private rituals. If she passes a spot where something bad could happen, she repeats a phrase under her breath five times—something her grandmother used to say about protection. She counts the seconds between red lights, and if the number lands on an unlucky integer, she starts over. She is certain that if she performs these mental routines correctly, she can prevent another accident from occurring. At the same time, she has begun to avoid any physical contact with passengers or coworkers. She does not shake hands, she angles her body away when someone reaches for a fare, and she flinches if her husband touches her unexpectedly in bed. Grief reminders are even harder: she cannot look at photographs of anyone who has died, including her own mother, because the pain of that loss merges with the guilt of the stranger’s death and becomes unbearable. Her husband has grown bewildered and hurt by her withdrawal. Their marriage, once warm, now operates at a careful distance.

At work, the consequences have accumulated. Elena used to enjoy the camaraderie of the depot, but now she eats lunch alone in her bus so no one will sit too close. She has asked to switch routes three times, trying to avoid intersections where she might see a crash, but there is no route in the city free of traffic. Her supervisor has noticed her jumpiness and has questioned her reliability. Elena does not tell anyone about the rituals or the flashbacks. She is not sure her life is worth living anymore—the weight of the guilt has made her wonder if continuing is even worthwhile. What finally brought her to seek help was a day last week when a child stumbled and scraped his knee on the sidewalk near her bus. The blood sent her into a full sensory reliving, and she had to pull over, shaking and crying, unable to drive for twenty minutes. The dispatch had to send a replacement. She was terrified that someone would see her as unstable, that she would lose her job, that the failure to protect would be exposed. She came to the clinic hoping to quiet the rituals and the memories, but what she is most afraid of is that the guilt will never lift—that she will always be the woman who sat still while someone died, and that no amount of counting or repeating will ever make it right.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Triggers: Lack of Control: The vignette does not describe a scenario where a lack of control triggers symptoms, though the patient reported this as a trigger.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
